name: Aleut
sweep_summary: Aleut is not in the catalog. All six title-keyword items (Taff 1992, Bergsland 1983, Rozelle 1997, Asinovsky & Golovko 1987, Oshima 1990, Oshima 1994; the Miyaoka & Endo 1994 record is a duplicate of Oshima 1994) turned out to be scanned online at the Alaska Native Language Archive (https://uafanlc.alaska.edu/Online/<id>/<id>.pdf; old uaf.edu URLs are dead, the record API is https://uafanlc.alaska.edu/drupal/api/record?identifier=<id> with an incomplete TLS chain) — all fetched sources, scanned (tesseract, 300 dpi, sequential) and read; plus Bergsland's 1997 reference grammar (ERIC microfiche text layer on archive.org) read at sec. 1.2.2.1. Everything is under with. Consistent picture: stress is non-phonemic and quantity/sonority-driven; Eastern Aleut = penultimate (mora) with a heavy final syllable attracting stress unless the penult is also heavy (Taff 1992 rule; Rozelle 1997 acoustic confirmation, stress assigned before final-syllable deletion; Oshima 1990/1994 'primary stress on the penultimate mora, secondary on the initial mora'); Atkan/Attuan = fluctuating with initial tendency (Bergsland 1983, 1997), and Asinovsky & Golovko 1987 claim Bering Island Aleut has no word stress, only an alternating rhythmic accent reset at long vowels. Only unread relevant item: Taff et al. 2001 J. Phonetics 29 (paywalled DOI 10.1006/jpho.2001.0142), medium priority.org, Crossref and the grammar's bibliography.

new_statements.quote: Stress is not phonemic. In so far as the initial syllable of polysyllabic words has frequently more than weakest stress, stress has a certain delimiting function. But it is largely determined by the relative sonority or weight of the syllables and/or by rhythmic factors ... In disyllabic word forms with a short final syllable the initial syllable, short or long, has the stronger stress in all the dialects, e.g. úla 'house', dálux 'wave'. In forms with a long vowel in the second syllable the stronger stress shifts to the final syllable ... In Eastern the stronger stress tends to fall on the next to the last syllable if the last one is short ... In Atkan the stronger stress tends to fall on the initial syllable of a trisyllabic form
new_statements.citation: Bergsland, Knut. 1997. Aleut Grammar: Unangam Tunuganaan Achixaasix (ANLC Research Paper 10). Fairbanks: Alaska Native Language Center.
new_statements.reading: Aleut word stress is non-phonemic and weight-driven (long vowel = heavy), with a dialect split at the right edge: Eastern (Umnak/Pribilof/Akutan) is penultimate by default, with a heavy (long-vowel) final syllable taking the stress unless the penult is also heavy (Taff 1992; Rozelle 1997 confirms acoustically; Oshima 1990/1994 state it as 'penultimate mora'), plus sonorant-consonant attraction and free variation; Atkan/Attuan (incl. Bering Island) is initial-leaning and fluctuating, and Asinovsky & Golovko 1987 deny word stress for Bering Island Aleut altogether in favour of an alternating rhythmic accent reset by long vowels. For a language-level coding: quantity-sensitive right-edge (penult, final if heavy) for Eastern; variable/initial for Atkan. Bergsland 1997 is the reference grammar and the most authoritative single statement; Taff 1992 pp. 137-143 is the explicit rule.

sources.citation: Bergsland, Knut. 1997. Aleut Grammar: Unangam Tunuganaan Achixaasix. A descriptive reference grammar of the Aleutian, Pribilof, and Commander Islands Aleut language (ANLC Research Paper 10). Fairbanks: Alaska Native Language Center. xiii+360 pp.

In disyllabic word forms with a short final syllable the initial syllable, short or long, has the stronger stress in all the dialects ... sources.locator: sec. 1.2.2.1 'Stress and quantity', pp. 30-31; sec. 1.6.1 'Emphatic stress', p. 45
sources.note: Reference grammar, all dialects: stress non-phonemic, weight/sonority- and rhythm-driven. Disyllables: initial unless the second vowel is long (then final). Eastern trisyllables: penultimate if the last syllable is short, but a sonorant consonant can pull it to the preceding syllable and initial stress is sometimes predominant. Atkan trisyllables: initial, pulled rightward by sonorants. Four-syllable words tend to a trochaic rhythm; long vowels attract stress in longer words. Emphatic stress on the initial syllable (p. 45).

sources.citation: Rozelle, Lorna. 1997. The effect of stress on vowel length in Aleut. UCLA Working Papers in Phonetics 95: 91-101.
sources.quote: Aleut has a quantity sensitive stress system. Taff (1992) states weight is assigned at the nuclear level so that consonants are weightless. Syllables containing long vowels are heavy, and syllables containing short vowels are light. Stress falls on the ultimate syllable if it is heavy and the penultimate syllable is light, (2a). Otherwise, stress falls on the penultimate syllable, (2b and 2c). [p.91] ... All vowels are short, and in each case, the vowel with greatest duration is the penultimate, not the antepenultimate, indicating that the penultimate syllable is stressed. Words receive stress before the final syllable is deleted. [p.97]
sources.locator: sec. 1.1 p. 91 (stress rule); sec. 3 pp. 95-96 (durations); sec. 4 p. 97 (final-syllable deletion); summary p. 99
sources.note: Acoustic study of four Pribilof Aleut speakers (data partly collected by Taff and Ladefoged). Restates Taff's rule: stress on a heavy (long-vowel) ultima, otherwise penultimate. Finds duration is a correlate of stress (short 64 -> 78 ms, long 130 -> 151 ms; ratio 1.2) without neutralising the length contrast, and that stress is assigned before final-syllable deletion (penult of the underlying form is the longest vowel). Concludes the measurements give 'phonetic verification of... Taff's stress rule'.

sources.citation: Oshima, Minoru. 1994. Prosody and Vowel Reduction in Eastern Aleut. In Osahito Miyaoka (ed.), Languages of the North Pacific Rim (Hokkaido University Publications in Linguistics 7), 149-158. Sapporo: Hokkaido University.
sources.quote: The Aleut (abbreviated as A) prosodic pattern has been considered rather simple when compared with its cognate Eskimo languages, because the primary stress (´) accent falls on the penultimate mora and the secondary stress (`) accent falls on the initial mora, with lengthening and gemination not being distinctive. [p.149] ... At the Conference in 1990 Knut Bergsland stated that stress is fluctuating and largely determined by vowel length and consonantic sonority and in EA it is frequently, but far from generally penultimate, while in Atka and Attu dialects it is more often initial. [p.149 fn.3]
sources.locator: sec. 0 Introduction p. 149 and footnotes 2-3; sec. 1.1 p. 151; sec. 2.2 p. 154 (cyclic even-mora stress)
sources.note: Eastern (Umnak) Aleut, fieldwork 1981-93: primary stress on the penultimate mora (so a final long vowel is stressed: i.láa), secondary stress on the initial mora; p.151 adds that the primary stress carries the pitch peak with a fall on the last mora, and that stress falls cyclically on even-numbered morae counting back from the penult. Uses this to derive the Eastern syncope rules. Records Bergsland's 1990 dissent (fluctuating, penultimate only 'frequently' in Eastern, initial more often in Atkan/Attuan).

sources.citation: Bergsland, Knut. 1983. Preliminary notes on Aleut prosody. Typescript dated December 9, 1983, 2 pp. Alaska Native Language Center.
sources.quote: Atkan (and Attuan). The stress is fluctuating, e.g. both 'ataqan and a'taqan, depending (presumably) on the rythm of the context. Usually, however, the initial syllable will have "some" stress, but the stress also depends upon the relative sonority of the syllables, that is, vowel length, e.g. ,a'daa (or 'a,daa) 'his/her father' vs. 'adang 'my father'; or consonantic sonority ... Eastern. In general, one could say, the penultimate "mora" (short vowel = 1 mora, long vowel = 2 more) has at least "some" stress, e.g. 'adang, a'daa, more or less as in Atkan. In tri- and quadrisyllabic forms, however, also the antepenult (mora) may have the main stress, and there is fluctuation
sources.note: First-hand field notes by the principal Aleut linguist. Atkan/Attuan: fluctuating, initial syllable usually has some stress, long vowels and sonorant consonants attract it. Eastern: the penultimate mora (long vowel = 2 morae, so a final long vowel is stressed) has at least some stress; antepenult may carry main stress in 3-4-syllable words; fluctuation; sentence rhythm also plays a part. Rest of the note is the Eastern syncope rule and sandhi.

sources.citation: Taff, Alice. 1992. Primary Stress in Aleut. University of Washington Working Papers in Linguistics 10 (supplement: Papers from NWLC VIII), pp. 137-145.
sources.quote: Aleut is one of the languages in which primary stress is too regular to have generated much analytical interest. Investigators have simply noted the predominately penultimate primary stress as well as some relationship between long vowels and stress. [p.137] ... Final syllables are stressed when heavy as in 4) ... unless the penult is also heavy as in 5). [pp.138-139] ... The best solution for assigning stress to Aleut words in citation form is 18): a. Assign moraic trochees from R->L iteratively b. with HFE (triggered by two final neighboring strong stresses) c. and application of End Rule Right. [p.143]
sources.locator: p. 137 (intro), p. 139 exx. 5-7, p. 143 rule (18); PDF pp. 3, 4, 9. p. 138 is partly covered by an archive card in the scan.
sources.note: Pribilof (Eastern) Aleut, tape-recorded data: quantity-sensitive (long vowel = heavy; codas weightless). Primary stress is penultimate; a heavy (long-vowel) final syllable takes it (su-kuún, sismikúu) unless the penult is also heavy (adáadaa). Formalised as moraic trochees R-to-L + End Rule Right + heavy-foot extrametricality. Truncated words keep penultimate stress (asxinúngin > asxínung). Author notes secondary stress and sentence-level shifts remain unanalysed and cites Geoghegan 1944:10 ('generally falls on the penult') and Bergsland 1956:39 ('not distinctive... rather fluctuating').

sources.citation: Oshima, Minoru. 1990. Prosody and Syncopation in Eastern Aleut. Papers from the Seventh Inuit Studies Conference, Fairbanks, 19-23 August 1990 (Inuit Studies Occasional Papers 4), 303-311.
sources.quote: The Aleut prosodic pattern of words has been considered rather simple, because the primary stress accent falls on the penultimate syllable or mora and the secondary stress accent falls on the initial syllable or mora, and lengthening and gemination are not distinctive unlike what is the case in Eskimo languages. [p.303] ... The stress accent cyclically falls on the even-numbered syllable backwards from the primarily stressed syllable in CV strings. As a result the odd-numbered syllable is unstressed and optionally (in a rapid speech style) syncopated. [p.305]
sources.locator: sec. 0 Introduction p. 303; sec. 3-2 Syncopation Rule 2 p. 305; sec. 5 Conclusion and fn. 1 p. 310
sources.note: Earlier version of Oshima 1994 (Umnak Eastern Aleut): primary stress penultimate syllable/mora, secondary initial; regressive alternating stress from the penult drives syncope. Footnote 1: Bergsland (1990) held that stress is largely determined by vowel length and consonantal sonority and unrelated to syncope.

sources.citation: Asinovsky, A. S. & E. V. Golovko. 1987. Rhythmic Accent Patterns in Aleut. Proceedings of the XIth International Congress of Phonetic Sciences, Tallinn, 1-7 August 1987, Se 8.5.1-8.5.3 (pp. 174-176).
sources.quote: Aleut, being a language without a word-stress, forms its rhythmic structure by means of two main things: rhythmic accent and long vowels. There are several main rhythmic accent patterns in Aleut, long vowels "breaking ranks" - then, rhythmic accent is counted from that "break". [p.174] ... In wordforms of CVCVC-structure (if they do not include long vowels), the first syllable is constantly accented ... In multi-syllable wordforms a rule of rhythmic accent puts an accent on every second syllable, except in the cases when a long vowel appears and breaks the rhythmic structure; then, rhythmic accent is counted from that "rhythmic break". [p.175]
sources.locator: Abstract and Introduction, Se 8.5.1 (p. 174); 'Accent and rhythmic structure', Se 8.5.2 (p. 175); conclusion Se 8.5.3 (p. 176)
sources.note: Bering Island (Commander Islands) Aleut = conservative Atkan dialect, fieldwork 1982 and 1985. Claims Aleut has no word stress: prominence is a rhythmic alternating accent (every second syllable, counted anew from each long vowel), CVCVC words accented on the first syllable, three-syllable words tend to accent the second; accent is governed by the syntactic stretch ('there are no prosodic means in Aleut which provide conditions for the wordform as an independent unit', p.176). Contradicts the penultimate-stress reading of Eastern Aleut but agrees with Bergsland on fluctuation and long-vowel a…
